summary: Defines a way for a DHCPv6 relay agent to give the server information that the server can pass on to the client, since relays cannot talk directly to clients. It also updates RFC 3315 by making explicit that relays must not modify the encapsulated payloads they forward back toward clients.

plainLanguage.summary: A messenger between two people sometimes knows helpful facts. This lets that go-between pass notes to the address-giving server, which then shares them with the device.

subtitle: How a DHCPv6 relay agent can hand the server options to pass along to the client.

tldr.problem: A DHCPv6 relay agent sometimes knows something the client needs, but relays cannot talk to clients directly and must deliver the server's reply unchanged.
tldr.mechanism: The relay wraps the options in a Relay-Supplied Options option (RSOO, code 66) inside its Relay-Forward message. The server may then copy those options into its own reply to the client.
tldr.outcome: Only options explicitly marked RSOO-enabled may travel this way, and relays still must not alter the reply payload on its way back. The RFC updates RFC 3315.

today: RFC 6422 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2011. It updates RFC 3315 by making explicit that relay agents must not modify encapsulation payloads relayed back toward clients, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Relays Need a Voice
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 specification (RFC 3315) lets relay agents forward messages between clients and servers that are not on the same IPv6 link. Sometimes the relay holds information the server does not have, but the client needs. The RFC's example is the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) local domain name, which the relay knows and the server does not.

DHCPv6 gives the relay no way to send options to the client. This document adds one: the relay proposes options to the server, and the server can send them on to the client.

This is not a general place to store client configuration in the relay. It targets specific cases where only the relay has the information, and it is meant for new specifications that need it.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the go-between knows a fact the device needs, but he is not allowed to talk to the device. This gives him a safe way to pass the fact along.

sections.title: Protocol Summary
sections.content:
DHCP clients cannot receive options directly from relay agents. The relay must deliver the payload from the server to the client without changing it.

So the relay sends its options to the server, encapsulated in a Relay-Supplied Options option (RSOO). The server can then choose to place those options in the response it sends to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay puts its note in an envelope addressed to the server. The server decides whether to copy the note into the letter for the device.

sections.title: The RSOO Encoding
sections.content:
The relay sends an RSOO in the Relay-Forward message. The option has the usual DHCPv6 option shape:

  • OPTION_RSOO: the option code, 66.
  • option-length: the length of the RSOO.
  • options: one or more DHCPv6 options that the relay wants the server to consider.
sections.plainLanguage: It is an envelope with a label saying what it is, how big it is, and the notes inside.

sections.title: RSOO-Enabled Options
sections.content:
The RSOO MUST NOT contain any option that is not specifically called out as an RSOO-enabled option. A specification that defines such an option MUST reference this RFC and MUST state that its option is RSOO-enabled. No DHCP option specified before this RFC is RSOO-enabled.

Such specifications must also ask IANA to add the option's name to the registry titled "Options Permitted in the Relay-Supplied Options Option", using text similar to the template the RFC provides.
sections.plainLanguage: Only notes on an approved list may go in the envelope. Anything not on the list is not allowed.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Relay agents. A relay MAY include an RSOO in a Relay-Forward message going toward the server. When relaying Relay-Reply payloads toward clients it MUST NOT modify them, and it MUST NOT put non-RSOO-enabled options in an RSOO. A relay that implements RSOO needs a configuration parameter that decides whether it will forward Relay-Forward messages containing an RSOO. If disabled, it MUST silently discard such messages, and it MUST examine all Relay-Forward encapsulations, not just the outer one.

Servers. A server MUST check each option inside an RSOO and MUST silently discard any that is not RSOO-enabled. It SHOULD have an administrator-configurable list of RSOO-enabled options, so new ones do not need a software update. It SHOULD add RSOO options for which it has no candidate of its own to its candidate list, and SHOULD discard those for which it already has one or more candidates. Then it builds the reply as usual under RFC 3315.

With nested Relay-Forward messages, conflicting values may arrive. The server MUST forward no more than one of them, and by default MUST choose the innermost value, from the relay closest to the client. Other heuristics are allowed if that remains the default.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay may pass notes but never rewrites the final letter. The server checks every note against the approved list, and if two relays disagree, it trusts the one closest to the device.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This mechanism lets a relay inject options into the server's response. In the known use cases, such as the ERP Local Domain Option (RFC 6440), RSOO-enabled options only ever originate on a relay and make little sense coming from a server.

A risk arises where the client side of an interface is untrusted and the network side is trusted. A malicious node acting as a relay on the untrusted side could supply an RSOO that overrides the same option from a trusted relay. In such environments administrators are advised to use relays that can drop Relay-Forward messages containing an RSOO, and to configure them to do so.

That only works if the server's message to the client is authenticated as in Section 21 of RFC 3315 or by a similar mechanism. Otherwise the malicious node can alter the server's response in transit and the client cannot detect it.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky stranger posing as a messenger could slip in a false note. Guards at the door can throw such notes away, and a signed letter lets the device spot tampering.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA assigned option code 66 (OPTION_RSOO) to the Relay-Supplied Options option, and created a registry titled "Options Permitted in the Relay-Supplied Options Option". Options may be added after IETF Review (RFC 5226).

That review should weigh the security implications of letting a relay supply the option's value. Where an IETF working group chartered to review DHCP extensions exists, review by some other working group is not sufficient.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of approved notes. Getting onto it takes a careful review, with extra attention to safety.

fields.name: options
fields.desc: One or more DHCPv6 options (variable length).
